chapter_title: Understanding Common Vulnerabilities: Access Control and Denial of Service

screens.title: Access Control & Denial of Service
screens.subtitle: Why who can call your functions — and how your code handles scale — determine contract safety

narration.text: In this lesson you’ll learn why access control and Denial of Service are foundational security problems for smart contracts. Access control mistakes let attackers assume administrative privileges or change critical variables simply by calling a public function. Denial of Service happens when contract logic becomes unusable, often because a loop or an external dependency requires more gas or cooperation than the system can guarantee. You will see clear, real-world examples: a contract that exposes setCriticalValue and transferOwnership without protection, and payout loops that can exceed the block gas limit. You’ll also learn secure alternatives: apply onlyOwner or role-based modifiers to protect sensitive functions, prefer pull-based payments or batch processing to avoid unbounded loops, and design for external failures by handling call failures gracefully and providing pause/unpause controls. By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify these vulnerabilities in code, apply idiomatic Solidity patterns to fix them, and explain why those fixes reduce risk. Think about one administrative function in a contract you’ve read — who should be able to call it and what would happen if anyone could?

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Secure contracts explicitly restrict who can perform critical actions and avoid single-transaction work that can exceed gas limits or depend on external success.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter — first set

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will identify common access control mistakes and implement basic protections. First, you will learn to spot missing modifiers like onlyOwner and public functions that should be restricted. You will see why a public setter on a critical variable is not harmless; it allows any caller to change contract behavior. Second, you will implement secure modifier-based access control in Solidity, and you will test it to ensure only the intended addresses can perform administrative actions. Each objective includes an example and a short mnemonic to help you apply the check when reviewing code. These skills matter because access control failures directly enable privilege escalation, incorrect state changes, and financial loss. A quick habit to form is: for every public or external function ask, who should call this, and what happens if anyone calls it? That question will guide your review and design choices.

screens.title: What is Access Control in Smart Contracts?
screens.subtitle: Ensuring only authorized actors change sensitive state

narration.text: Access control means explicitly defining who may call specific functions or change state within a contract. A common pattern is the onlyOwner modifier, which checks that the caller equals a stored owner address. This sounds simple, but the practical risk appears when developers add new functions without adding the appropriate check. For example, a public setter for a critical value or a public transferOwnership function allows any external actor to assume admin privileges or corrupt contract logic. A concrete example from the chapter shows setCriticalValue and transferOwnership left public; an attacker can call transferOwnership to become owner, then change critical variables. A common misconception is assuming that a function won’t be abused because its logic is benign, or that only trusted scripts will call it. In reality, the EVM treats all callers equally, so you must be explicit and defensive. When you implement access control, also check for edge cases: the zero address for new owner, and making sure modifiers are applied consistently to all functions that change critical state. As a takeaway, make it a code-review rule to list every public or external function and document who should be able to call it. Which public function in your recent code review would you flag for an access-control check?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Access control requires explicit, auditable checks that restrict functions to authorized roles or addresses.

content.html:
Core Concept
Access Control
Control who can alter critical state and perform administrative actions in your contract.
Why it matters: prevents privilege escalation and unauthorized asset manipulation.
Common mistake: adding public setters without modifiers.
Good habit: audit every public/external function and record intended callers.
Vulnerable example (excerpt)
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract VulnerableAccessControl {
    address public owner;
    uint256 public criticalValue;

    constructor() {
        owner = msg.sender;
        criticalValue = 100;
    }

    // VULNERABLE: Anyone can change the critical value
    function setCriticalValue(uint256 _newValue) public {
        criticalValue = _newValue;
    }

    // VULNERABLE: Anyone can transfer ownership
    function transferOwnership(address _newOwner) public {
        owner = _newOwner;
    }

    modifier onlyOwner() {
        require(msg.sender == owner, "Not owner");
        _;
    }
}
Misconception
Assuming a function is safe because its intent is benign. Attackers don't respect intent.
Takeaway
Always protect state-changing functions with explicit checks and test them under multiple caller addresses.

screens.title: Applying onlyOwner: fix the vulnerable example
screens.subtitle: How modifiers prevent unauthorized calls

narration.text: A straightforward and widely-used protection is the onlyOwner modifier. It stores an owner address and gates sensitive functions with a require check. This pattern is clear, minimal, and easy to audit — but it can be limiting for multi-admin systems. The chapter gives a secure rewrite of the vulnerable contract where setCriticalValue and transferOwnership are protected by onlyOwner. The secure version also checks for a zero address when transferring ownership. When you read the secure example, notice the pattern: check the caller first, then update state. That ordering makes bugs less likely. A common follow-up is: when should you move to role-based access control? If multiple distinct responsibilities are required — for example, one address should mint tokens while another can pause the contract — RBAC provides separate grants and clearer governance. For single-administrator scenarios, onlyOwner is sufficient and compact. The practical advice is to implement onlyOwner quickly, then evaluate RBAC if your dApp requires multiple trusted roles. As you code, write tests that assert transactions revert from unauthorized addresses and succeed for the owner. How would you write a test that ensures transferOwnership cannot be called by a random account?

keyIdea.title: Pattern
keyIdea.text: Use onlyOwner to gate sensitive state changes, validate inputs, and test authorization paths.

content.html:
Definition
onlyOwner modifier
A small, auditable check that prevents unauthorized callers from executing sensitive functions.
Test: add an unauthorized caller test to assert require failure for protected functions.
When to use
Single-owner contracts, administrative tasks, and emergency controls.
When to consider RBAC
If you need many admins with different responsibilities, RBAC scales better than a single owner address.
Secure example (excerpt)
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract SecureAccessControl {
    address public owner;
    uint256 public criticalValue;

    constructor() {
        owner = msg.sender;
        criticalValue = 100;
    }

    modifier onlyOwner() {
        require(msg.sender == owner, "Not owner");
        _;
    }

    // SECURE: Only the owner can change the critical value
    function setCriticalValue(uint256 _newValue) public onlyOwner {
        criticalValue = _newValue;
    }

    // SECURE: Only the owner can transfer ownership
    function transferOwnership(address _newOwner) public onlyOwner {
        require(_newOwner != address(0), "New owner cannot be zero address");
        owner = _newOwner;
    }
}
Takeaway
Apply checks first, validate inputs like zero address, and keep modifier usage consistent across all sensitive functions.

screens.title: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)
screens.subtitle: When a single owner is not enough

narration.text: Role-Based Access Control lets you define separate permissions and grant them to multiple addresses. Instead of a single owner, you create roles such as MINTER_ROLE and PAUSER_ROLE, and functions check role membership before proceeding. The advantage is finer-grained authority and reduced operational risk: one compromised key does not automatically grant every privilege. The chapter refers to OpenZeppelin's AccessControl as a robust implementation pattern: it stores role data and provides grant and revoke functions. A practical misconception is assuming RBAC is more complex and unnecessary; in many systems RBAC simplifies governance because roles can be assigned to multisig or DAO-controlled addresses. When designing RBAC, document which role is allowed to call which functions, and prefer granting roles to contracts or multisigs rather than ephemeral external accounts. Also include revoke paths for key rotation. To practice, refactor an onlyOwner contract to use separate roles for administration and emergency pausing. How would you assign a pauser role in deployment to a multisig? Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) means rbac provides granular permissions that map to organizational responsibilities, reducing blast radius when keys are compromised.. In practical terms, when a single owner is not enough. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Why RBAC
keyIdea.text: RBAC provides granular permissions that map to organizational responsibilities, reducing blast radius when keys are compromised.

content.html:
Process Flow
RBAC steps
  1. Define roles that reflect responsibilities, e.g., MINTER_ROLE, PAUSER_ROLE.
  2. Grant roles to addresses or multisigs at deployment or via governance.
  3. Check role membership in function modifiers before executing sensitive logic.
  4. Revoke or rotate roles when keys are retired.
Tip: Assign roles to multisigs or governance contracts, not to single personal keys.
Visual: role mapping
MINTER_ROLE
Can mint tokens
PAUSER_ROLE
Can pause/unpause contract
AUDITOR_ROLE
Can read and trigger governance checks
Multisig
Recommended grantee for sensitive roles
Takeaway
Design roles to minimize privileges and attach them to governance-friendly addresses. RBAC increases clarity and reduces single-point-of-failure risk.

screens.title: Denial of Service (DoS) in Smart Contracts
screens.subtitle: How contracts become unusable and why it matters

narration.text: A Denial of Service attack aims to make a contract or a function unusable for legitimate users. In smart contracts this commonly happens when a function tries to process an unbounded amount of work — for example iterating through an ever-growing array — and eventually the transaction requires more gas than a single block allows. At that point the function will always revert and become effectively disabled. The chapter gives a clear vulnerable example: payoutAll iterates over participants and performs transfers, which will fail once the participants array grows too large. Another DoS source is external call dependencies — if your contract requires a third-party contract or an oracle to respond, and that external call fails or is paused, your contract could be blocked. A misconception is thinking DoS only comes from malicious users; it can also arise from legitimate growth of data structures that you did not cap. The right approach is to design for scale: prefer pull payments, batch processing, or off-chain aggregation. Also instrument your contract with pause controls so you can stop operations while migrating or fixing a DoS condition. How would you test a payout loop against scale on a local network?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: DoS occurs when contract operations require more gas or external cooperation than the system can guarantee, making them unusable.

content.html:
Core Concept
Denial of Service
When contract logic becomes unusable due to gas limits or failing external dependencies.
Why it happens: unbounded loops and fragile external calls.
Practical sign: a function that reverts only once an array grows beyond a certain size.
Defense: pull payments, batch processing, and pause controls.
Vulnerable payout example
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract VulnerableDoS {
    address[] public participants;
    mapping(address => uint256) public balances;

    function addParticipant(address _participant) public {
        participants.push(_participant);
    }

    // VULNERABLE: Unbounded loop, can run out of gas if participants array is too large
    function payoutAll() public {
        for (uint i = 0; i < participants.length; i++) {
            address participant = participants[i];
            // Imagine sending Ether here
            // (bool success, ) = participant.call{value: balances[participant]}("");
            // require(success, "Transfer failed");
            // balances[participant] = 0;
        }
    }
}
Takeaway
Never perform unbounded work in a single transaction; design to spread cost or move work off-chain.

screens.title: Pull Payments vs Push Payments
screens.subtitle: Shift gas cost and avoid unbounded iterations

narration.text: A powerful pattern to avoid DoS via unbounded loops is the pull payment. Instead of pushing funds to many recipients in a single transaction, the contract records owed balances and each recipient calls withdraw to claim funds. This shifts gas costs to claimants and ensures no single transaction must touch every recipient. The chapter suggests pull payments or batch processing as two principal mitigations. Batch processing splits work across multiple transactions and requires careful indexing and bounds checking. A common misconception is that pull payments always remove risk; they shift who pays gas and require safe accounting to prevent double withdrawals. Also, push-to-pull refactors should follow the checks-effects-interactions pattern, updating balances before making external calls. The practical choice depends on UX trade-offs: pull payments require users to initiate a claim, while push payments can be more convenient but fragile at scale. As a quick exercise, convert a payoutAll function into a simple withdraw pattern where balances are stored and users call withdraw. What new tests would you add to ensure no double-spend occurs? Pull Payments vs Push Payments means pull payments shift gas to recipients and avoid single-transaction iteration; batch processing spreads work across transactions when needed.. In practical terms, shift gas cost and avoid unbounded iterations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Defense comparison
keyIdea.text: Pull payments shift gas to recipients and avoid single-transaction iteration; batch processing spreads work across transactions when needed.

content.html:
Comparison
Pull vs Push
Pull: recipients call withdraw; contract stores balances; avoids unbounded loops.
Push: contract iterates and sends; can be simpler but vulnerable to gas limits.
Batch: process a slice of items per transaction with start and count parameters.
Takeaway
Prefer pull payments for high-cardinality payouts; use batching when pull semantics are unsuitable for UX reasons.
Pattern: simple withdraw
// Conceptual withdraw pattern
mapping(address => uint256) public balances;

function depositFor(address to) internal {
  balances[to] += msg.value;
}

function withdraw() public {
  uint256 amount = balances[msg.sender];
  require(amount > 0, "No funds");
  balances[msg.sender] = 0; // effects first
  (bool success, ) = msg.sender.call{value: amount}("");
  require(success, "Transfer failed");
}
Common tests
Assert balances zero after withdraw, assert only intended recipient can withdraw their balance, simulate failed transfers and ensure state remains consistent.

screens.title: External Call Dependencies and DoS
screens.subtitle: Why relying on others can make your contract fragile

narration.text: External call dependencies occur when your contract's critical action depends on another contract or account to behave correctly. Examples include requiring an oracle to update a price before proceeding or sending Ether to recipients whose fallback functions may revert. If the external contract is paused, malicious, or intentionally reverted, your dependent function can fail. One illustration from the chapter notes that using call to transfer funds can fail if the recipient's fallback reverts, and if that transfer is part of a larger atomic operation it can block the whole transaction. A common misconception is trusting third-party contracts implicitly. Instead, assume external calls can fail, and code defensively: isolate external interactions, update local state before making calls (checks-effects-interactions), and design alternate flows when essential external services are unavailable. Consider adding timeouts, retry patterns, or pause controls to handle prolonged external failures. For every external dependency, ask: what happens if it is unavailable for an hour, a day, or forever? That question should shape how you expose features that rely on others. External Call Dependencies and DoS means treat external calls as potentially failing: update state first, handle errors, and avoid making contract liveness depend on third parties.. In practical terms, why relying on others can make your contract fragile. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Defense
keyIdea.text: Treat external calls as potentially failing: update state first, handle errors, and avoid making contract liveness depend on third parties.

content.html:
Core Concept
External Call Dependencies
If a critical action depends on an external contract, failures there can DoS your contract.
Risk: external contract paused or maliciously reverting.
Mitigation: checks-effects-interactions and pull/batch patterns.
Operational: add pause/unpause when external services are unreliable.
Practical patterns
  • Update state before external calls to avoid inconsistent balances.
  • Use pull payments when sending funds to unknown recipients.
  • Provide fallback or admin options if essential external services fail.
Check
List each external dependency and document failure modes and an operational response for each.

screens.title: Voting Contract: Vulnerable vs Secure
screens.subtitle: Hands-on example to apply access control and DoS fixes

narration.text: The chapter’s hands-on activity centers on a Voting contract. The vulnerable version allows anyone to add proposals and uses a tallyVotes function that iterates over all proposals — two clear security problems. Anyone can add proposals, which lets attackers spam or manipulate choices; and tallyVotes as written risks DoS if proposals grow very large. The secure version introduces an onlyAdmin modifier to restrict adding proposals and removes the unbounded tallyVotes in favor of a getProposalVoteCount function and off-chain tallying. The educational point is not that tallying must be done on-chain, but that you should avoid operations that grow unboundedly and depend on single-transaction completion. For the hands-on task, deploy both contracts locally and write tests showing an unauthorized user can add proposals in the vulnerable contract but is rejected in the secure one. Also, document how the vulnerable tallyVotes could fail if proposals become large, and propose either off-chain tallying or a rewarded actor who processes limited batches to finalize results. Which approach would you choose for a trusted DAO versus a low-trust environment? Voting Contract: Vulnerable vs Secure means practice converting open access to restricted access and recognize unbounded loops as dos risks in a concrete voting example.. In practical terms, hands-on example to apply access control and dos fixes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Exercise goal
keyIdea.text: Practice converting open access to restricted access and recognize unbounded loops as DoS risks in a concrete voting example.

content.html:
Practice
VulnerableVoting (starter)
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract VulnerableVoting {
    struct Proposal {
        string name;
        uint256 voteCount;
    }

    Proposal[] public proposals;
    address public admin;

    constructor() {
        admin = msg.sender;
    }

    // VULNERABLE: Anyone can add proposals
    function addProposal(string memory _name) public {
        proposals.push(Proposal(_name, 0));
    }

    function vote(uint256 _proposalId) public {
        require(_proposalId < proposals.length, "Invalid proposal ID");
        proposals[_proposalId].voteCount++;
    }

    // VULNERABLE: Unbounded loop for tallying
    function tallyVotes() public view returns (uint256 winningProposalId) {
        uint256 maxVotes = 0;
        winningProposalId = 0;

        for (uint i = 0; i < proposals.length; i++) {
            if (proposals[i].voteCount > maxVotes) {
                maxVotes = proposals[i].voteCount;
                winningProposalId = i;
            }
        }
        return winningProposalId;
    }
}
Secure version
SecureVoting (approach)
// SecureVoting: onlyAdmin and no unbounded tally
// Conceptual changes: add onlyAdmin modifier, remove tallyVotes, expose getProposalVoteCount

// In SecureVoting:
// function addProposal(string memory _name) public onlyAdmin { ... }
// function getProposalVoteCount(uint256 _proposalId) public view returns (uint256) { ... }
Testing hints
Write tests that show an unauthorized account is reverted when calling addProposal on SecureVoting, and that VulnerableVoting allows it. Also simulate large proposal arrays to reason about tallyVotes failing.

screens.title: Batch Processing as a DoS Mitigation
screens.subtitle: Split work into bounded-sized transactions

narration.text: Batch processing is another effective technique to handle large datasets without exceeding gas limits. Instead of a single transaction iterating an entire array, implement a function that processes a slice defined by startIndex and count. Each call handles a fixed amount of work and updates progress, allowing an administrator or an incentivized actor to complete the full operation across multiple transactions. The chapter presents a batch withdraw example that requires a bounds check and uses checks-effects-interactions: update balances and indices before making external calls. A frequent misconception is that batching removes all friction; it introduces state-tracking and requires careful bounds checking to avoid out-of-bounds errors. Also consider who will finish the batches: you may incentivize a worker or allow anyone to call batch processing. When designing batches, choose a conservative count parameter that keeps gas usage well under typical block gas limits, and add tests that run the batch repeatedly until completion. What invariant must you preserve between batch calls to ensure consistency? Batch Processing as a DoS Mitigation means process in bounded batches with explicit start and count arguments and checks to keep each transaction within gas limits.. In practical terms, split work into bounded-sized transactions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pattern
keyIdea.text: Process in bounded batches with explicit start and count arguments and checks to keep each transaction within gas limits.

content.html:
Process Flow
Batch processing
Split large operations into repeated bounded transactions to avoid gas limits.
  1. Caller provides startIndex and count.
  2. Validate bounds: startIndex + count <= array.length.
  3. Loop from startIndex to endIndex and perform safe, limited work.
  4. Update progress state to record completed ranges.
Takeaway
Batches give you predictable gas costs and allow the system to make progress even as data grows.
Batch example (concept)
function withdrawInBatch(uint256 _startIndex, uint256 _count) public onlyOwner {
    uint256 endIndex = _startIndex + _count;
    require(endIndex <= beneficiaries.length, "Batch out of bounds");

    for (uint i = _startIndex; i < endIndex; i++) {
        address b = beneficiaries[i];
        uint256 amt = balances[b];
        if (amt > 0) {
            balances[b] = 0; // effect first
            (bool success, ) = b.call{value: amt}("");
            require(success, "Transfer failed");
        }
    }
}
Testing tip
Simulate batch calls in tests and assert the state after each call to ensure no items are missed or double-processed.

screens.title: Checklist: Preventing Access Control & DoS Failures
screens.subtitle: A practical audit checklist you can apply now

narration.text: When reviewing or designing contracts, a short checklist helps prevent common failures. First, enumerate all public and external functions and document the intended caller and effect of each. Second, ensure every sensitive function has an explicit access check, validate inputs like non-zero addresses, and add tests that assert reverts for unauthorized callers. Third, review loops and collection-processing functions; if their cost grows with use, refactor to pull payments or batch processing. Fourth, list external dependencies and design fallback or pause strategies for each; never assume an oracle or payment endpoint will always succeed. Fifth, prefer RBAC for multi-role systems and attach roles to multisigs or governance-managed contracts when possible. Finally, instrument emergency controls like pause/unpause and ensure they are themselves protected. Practical misconceptions to avoid: thinking that internal code flow limits callers implicitly, or believing fixed gas heuristics will always hold as the network evolves. Use automated tests and local simulations for scale and failure modes. Which two items from this checklist will you add to your next audit? Checklist: Preventing Access Control & DoS Failures means enumerate public functions, validate access, avoid unbounded work, handle external failures, and prefer rbac for complex permissioning.. In practical terms, a practical audit checklist you can apply now. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Audit checklist
keyIdea.text: Enumerate public functions, validate access, avoid unbounded work, handle external failures, and prefer RBAC for complex permissioning.

content.html:
Best Practices
Security Checklist

List all public/external functions and intended callers.
Protect setters
Apply onlyOwner or role checks and validate inputs like addresses.
Avoid unbounded loops
Use pull payments or batching for large collections.
Handle external calls
Assume failures and design graceful fallbacks or pause mechanisms.
Use RBAC
Assign roles and prefer multisigs for sensitive permissions.
Test DoS scenarios
Simulate large arrays, failing external calls, and partial batch processing.
Key Takeaway

Make access rules explicit, avoid unbounded single-transaction work, and design for external failures. Audit and test these assumptions regularly.

narration.text: Before you move on, keep six compact ideas top of mind. First, Access Control limits who can call functions and must be explicit. Second, the onlyOwner modifier is a simple check that gates critical actions and is useful for single-admin flows. Third, Role-Based Access Control assigns named roles to multiple addresses for finer permissioning. Fourth, Denial of Service occurs when contract operations become unusable, commonly because of gas limits on loops or failing external calls. Fifth, Unbounded Loops iterate over ever-growing collections and can render a function unusable when gas runs out. Sixth, a Pull Payment System shifts the gas burden to recipients who call withdraw, preventing mass push operations from failing. These concise concepts map directly to the chapter examples and should guide both design and code reviews. Key Concepts means think: who can call this? could this grow without bound? who pays the gas?. In practical terms, compact definitions to recall quickly. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. content.html:
Key Concepts
Access Control
Mechanisms that restrict who can call functions or change state.
onlyOwner
A simple modifier restricting a function to the contract owner address.
RBAC
Assign named roles to addresses for granular, multi-admin permissions.
Denial of Service
Attacks or conditions that make a contract’s functions unusable.
Unbounded Loops
Loops over growing collections that can exceed block gas limits and revert.
Pull Payment System
Recipients withdraw owed funds themselves, preventing large push loops.
Summary

Make permissions explicit and design operations to remain callable as your system scales.

narration.text: These final reminders are short, actionable rules you can apply immediately: always protect setters with explicit checks; if a function processes many items, prefer pull or batch approaches; treat external calls as potentially failing and add emergency pause controls; prefer RBAC for multiple responsibilities and attach roles to multisigs or governance where possible. When auditing, add tests that simulate large collections and failing external calls. These concrete steps will help you avoid the most common access control and DoS pitfalls covered in this chapter.
